Tech Report: Bundesliga treat Harry Kane's Ballon d'Or as beacon of hope as Germany's competitiveness questions linger

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2127 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even if the hints of a smile never fully leave his face, there is an overriding sense of practicality when Philipp Lahm speaks.
  • In a recent development, "It helped Harry Kane and Michael Olise that they came from another country," Lahm mentioned four days after Kane's big win.
  • Recent findings suggest that A quick glance at the data would confirm the hypothesis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even if the hints of a smile never fully leave his face, there is an overriding sense of practicality when Philipp Lahm speaks. He seems to have shed the intensity associated with the life of a professional athlete nearly a decade after retiring, but the characteristics of a World Cup-winning captain are hard to miss. He is friendly and open but also serious, so when the topic of conversation shifts to Harry Kane's Ballon d'Or triumph, he is politely unflinching in his assessment of what the award means for soccer in Germany.

In a recent development, "It helped Harry Kane and Michael Olise that they came from another country," Lahm mentioned four days after Kane's big win. "I think it's quite difficult for a German player playing in the Bundesliga [to win the Ballon d'Or].".

Recent findings suggest that A quick glance at the data would confirm the hypothesis. The last Bundesliga-based player and the last German player to win the sport's most prestigious individual award was Borussia Dortmund's Matthias Sammer in 1996. A German player has only finished inside the top three of the Ballon d'Or three times since, the last being Manuel Neuer in 2014, while Kane is only the seventh Bundesliga player to rank in the top three since Sammer's win. Lahm seamlessly links the pattern to another less-than-ideal trend in Germany's top flight -- Bayern Munich, with whom he won eight Bundesliga titles, are the division's indisputable kings.

They have lost the title just once since the 2012-13 season, a lack of competitiveness at the top of the table a natural consequence of their dominance. This is, in some ways, not Bayern's problem, but a narrative persists in Germany regardless. Players have historically been unable to reach the peaks of the game in Germany because of the circumstances, inspiring a wide-ranging set of side effects. Kane's move to Bayern was not designed to be anything other than the right move at the right time for a player talented enough to compete for the UEFA Champions League, but three years later, those invested in the Bundesliga's success are beginning to treat him as a beacon of hope.

"I do hope that the good players stay in the Bundesliga," Lahm said, "so I'm hopeful through Harry Kane that a lot of other players will follow because it's possible to win and play here.".

According to recent reports, the argument to join Bayern Munich is a straightforward one, if you ask sporting director Christoph Freund -- "you can win titles with us," both in Germany and Europe. Bayern have won the Champions League twice in the last 14 years, a feat matched only by Paris Saint-Germain and topped by Real Madrid. The Bundesliga's distribution of wealth favors them in this case, to the point that it likely played a sizable role in signing Kane and Olise. The balance of financial power in the European club game, though, has shifted as Bayern re-established their foothold in Germany -- the Premier League has become the sport's league of choice because it has the financial might to back up the claim. Players like Robert Lewandowski and Mario Gotze used to prove their worth at other German clubs (and in their specific case, Borussia Dortmund) before climbing up the food chain and joining Bayern. Florian Wirtz's jump from Bayer Leverkusen to Liverpool in 2025, though, is an example of a new world order, one some hope Kane's Ballon d'Or might change.

Industry observers note that "It's all about the attention, so when you're successful with the German national team that's visible, but then when you play also successful soccer with Liverpool, then the attention in U.K. is much bigger," Lahm said, citing Wirtz's hypothetical Ballon d'Or case as an example, "so that would be more difficult for a German player in the Bundesliga alone, rather than changing to somewhere else outside and being successful abroad.".

The Bundesliga's international appeal has not only taken a hit on the sporting side in recent years. Bayern's executives believe their club makes up around 50% of the league's brand value globally, and though they are unapologetic about their strengths on the pitch, they also argue they are doing too much of the heavy lifting. Rouven Kasper, a member of Bayern's executive board, pointed to Premier League clubs' oversized presence on preseason tours as a primary example for the Bundesliga to follow but all but questioned the league's interest in the strategy.

Sources indicate that "The league needs to be, as well, stronger and bring more reach, but the league exists from the clubs," Kasper said. "We are the spearhead of German football, and I think together with the other clubs and together with the league, we need to be even more active in the markets ... it's not enough, and at the end, it's about people, community. We want to be approachable. We want to talk to the people. We want to be there, as the Bundesliga and Bayern alone cannot do it together with Dortmund, so we need more activities from the league and being in different markets, as the U.K. guys are doing and also the Spanish guys are doing. We will do our part.".

Their part includes potentially using Kane as a hook for player recruitment, even if other leagues have their charms for the world's top talents.

According to recent reports, "I think everybody knows the Premier League is the biggest league at the moment," Freund said. "Also, Spain is really attractive with Real Madrid and Barcelona, but we know we are Bayern Munich and the German Bundesliga is also really a strong league, a really good league, outstanding stadiums, outstanding atmosphere, and you can [perform] also on a very high level like Harry, the next step in his career, and therefore, I think Bayern Munich and also the German Bundesliga is very attractive, also, for international top players.".

It has been revealed that some in the Bundesliga, though, are resigned to the fact that there are certain things Bayern -- and other European clubs -- will simply beat them to. Dortmund have held strong in their attempts to mount a title challenge this season, level on points with Bayern after eight games thanks to Saturday's 2-2 draw in Der Klassiker. For the foreseeable future, though, recruitment of elite talents cannot and will not play a central role in their quest to win silverware. "We never refuse, or we never avoid to tell you guys where we are from, but in comparison to Munich, Madrid, London, Paris, Milan, we are from Dortmund and from a purely economic perspective, we are far behind them," Borussia Dortmund CEO Carsten Cramer noted. "If they [are] just interested in trophies and silver, if they look for the Ballon d'Or player wearing a black and yellow shirt, maybe that is something we can't offer to them.".

While Bayern's brand is wrapped in the quiet luxury of their domestic stronghold, Cramer argued that Dortmund's appeal is a qualitative one.

It has been revealed that "In the last 13 years, we didn't become champion but though we didn't become champion, the interest in Dortmund is still increasing and the amount of people following our club on social media and wherever we travel in the world is quite huge," he stated. "We are able to offer a different approach: closeness. That is the Dortmund way, and I think that is maybe one of the reasons that many, many hardcore supporters of one club do have a sympathy for us as a second-love club, which I do not complain about, and that is our way. I don't want to make us too small by saying we are a niche club, but we are for sure a bit different, and I don't complain about [it].".

Patrick Owomoyela, a defender for Jurgen Klopp's Dortmund team that won back-to-back Bundesliga titles more than a decade ago, can clearly map out the recipe to beat Bayern to the top. Strong squad composition and compatibility go a long way, and he believes the current iteration of Dortmund has that -- he praised head coach Niko Kovac's defensive structure and commended him for "sprinkling the creativity" into the team in the months since taking the job in January 2025. There is just one problem, though.

In a recent development, "Even though you know the recipe, the soup is not always the same," he noted. "Even though you put in the same ingredients, it's not always tasting the same, and if it does, maybe it's not the perfect soup, you know? So you need to find that special something.".

Recent findings suggest that much like Cramer, Owomoyela has a qualitative argument of his own to make when it comes to breaking Bayern's decades-long dominance in the Bundesliga. The "special something" for his Dortmund team was a sense of camaraderie, the foundation of which was Klopp's joyous approach, though he openly admitted that is a difficult thing to replicate.

"This is sometimes the mentality of the guys or the personality of the guys and how that fits together, on top of the stuff that they can do with the ball and as I said, we weren't the best in terms of playing football," he said. "We were the best team. We had the most fun. We really liked doing a lot of stuff together. We were like a family, and you don't find that all the time, and it gets harder, I would say, every year because football has changed. The plans of players nowadays are totally different ... These guys have a plan, so they want to be part of something for this period of time, but then they want to move on, and that makes it, of course, hard to find that chemistry because he is gone next year.".

It has been revealed that it is the concern he identified with Leverkusen, the Bundesliga's last champion not named Bayern. Their rise up the ranks in the 2023-24 season was ambitious and impressive, but two years later, the mainstays of their title-winning campaign were elsewhere. Wirtz left for Liverpool, as did Jeremie Frimpong, Granit Xhaka now finds himself at Sunderland, Piero Hincapie now plays for Arsenal and then-head coach Xabi Alonso made a stop at Real Madrid before landing at his current post at Chelsea. Jonathan Tah, meanwhile, went the old-school route and now plays at Bayern. The next challenger to Bayern's throne will likely face the same fate for the foreseeable future, no matter whether its stars move to Munich or settle in England.

Sources indicate that saturday's draw between Bayern and Dortmund, though, has offered a flicker of optimism that the Bundesliga might have a title race on its hands before the next great team gets stripped for parts. The 2-2 scoreline flatters Dortmund -- Bayern racked up 4.48 expected goals and were unlucky when the crossbar denied them on both Kane's second-half penalty and a late strike from Lennart Karl, while the visitors generated just 0.74 xG. Owomoyela argued, though, that Bayern have their flaws.

According to recent reports, "What's it gonna take to take that away from Bayern after all these years again?" he asked. "It's just to believe that it's possible and I think the Bayern team demonstrated in this season as well, or especially maybe, that you can wound them, you can hurt them and something is possible. You can see that in almost every game they played, even in that cup game [against second-division side Magdeburg on Oct. 28] that they just had and they won it 6-1 ... They hit the post, hit the crossbar, scored a goal, had two other massive chances so now take a team with more quality, with the right kind of belief, there might be something possible.".

Saturday's Klassiker only added to the Bundesliga's week of good news, presenting a different case of the league's strengths than Kane's Ballon d'Or triumph, one that will likely take precedence in the short term. The longer Dortmund keep pace with Bayern, the more intriguing the Bundesliga becomes, and at this stage of the season, the possibility of a genuine title race is easy enough to dream up. That sense of optimism, though, tends to give way to the league's current realities. Even if Dortmund answered the question in the affirmative once, there's a long way to go until anyone can definitively say that Bayern can be topped.

Sources indicate that "We weren't really eye-level competitors," Owomoyela said about Dortmund's ability to compete with Bayern in the years since their back-to-back Bundesliga titles. "We were there and we were able to hunt, but from a little distance, and I think everybody understands that.".

From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs, and why the connection is complicated

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes.
  • But as Americans vote in the US midterm elections, it's time to think about how disgust shapes our politics, or whether our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?
  • The smell of rotten food can make us recoil.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes.

But as Americans vote in the US midterm elections, it's time to think about how disgust shapes our politics, or whether our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.

One explanation begins with evolution.

"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.

But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:.

One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.

"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

Industry observers note that indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe.".

Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.

"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar mentioned.

Industry observers note that disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.

A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.

However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.

Some early studies suggested conservatives demonstrated stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.

Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.

"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.

Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.

"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it.".

The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility.".

They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.

But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.

What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

"People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.

Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.

He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.

Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.

"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar remarked.

The newly introduced study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.

Recent findings suggest that inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best.".

Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.

In a recent development, "I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.

Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he remarked.

The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.

"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.

Sources indicate that inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.

"It's one of the many influences on people's politics.".

Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.

He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.

"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said. Edited by: Rosalie Delaney.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • At half-time, Manchester United looked down and out and Michael Carrick’s reign as manager as good as finished.
  • Roma were 2-0 in front and coasting, gorging on a desperate United’s litany of errors, and there was full-scale mutiny in the stands at Old Trafford.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So maybe there is some fight left in the old dog yet?

At half-time, Manchester United looked down and out and Michael Carrick’s reign as manager as good as finished.

Roma were 2-0 in front and coasting, gorging on a desperate United’s litany of errors, and there was full-scale mutiny in the stands at Old Trafford. A fifth defeat in six matches and the club’s longest winless run for 48 years beckoned. It was toxic on and off the pitch.

And then something changed. United, from being a dishevelled, disorganised mess, suddenly seemed to remember who they were supposed to be and what they were supposed to represent. Surrender gave way to fight. A team that had been feeling sorry for themselves discovered some pride. A crowd that had been baying for blood turned Old Trafford into a bear pit of a very different kind, and Roma simply did not know what had hit them.

This club have served up some famous comebacks over the decades, but it was hard to think of too many occasions when the mood and momentum had shifted this violently from one half to the next.

United fans were in open revolt in that first half, releasing green and gold balloons in protests before kick-off and then throwing tennis balls on to the pitch amid furious chanting against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. The players looked like they would rather have been anywhere else.

And yet by the 86th minute Matheus Cunha’s wild celebrations were encapsulating a wild night, the Brazilian ripping off his shirt after his dramatic winner before launching himself into a delirious crowd drunk on the euphoria of a victory that had seemed improbable in the extreme at the interval, when boos cascaded from the stands.

According to recent reports, whether this proves little more than a thrilling, heroic interlude in the endgame for Carrick, or the start of a genuine turnaround, is hard to know. And, let’s be clear, there was so much about the first-half performance to concern the hierarchy, who came under persistent, furious attack from fans at war with an ownership it reviles and wants gone.

But the second half stood firmly at odds with the shambolic display that had preceded it and suggested all may not be quite lost just yet.

Aston Villa visit Old Trafford on Sunday in the final game before the international break and, if Carrick can follow this with another win, then it will be intriguing to see where the Old Trafford board goes from there.

In a recent development, carrick may at least have been encouraged by some of the things Bruno Fernandes stated after the game, not least that he warranted being dropped against Bournemouth. And it was the captain who kick-started the fightback against Roma, albeit at the second attempt.

He had won the penalty after being fouled by Gianluca Mancini only to then contrive to miss it. But a retake was ordered for encroachment and, given a second bite at the cherry, Fernandes made no mistake.

NO MISTAKE THIS TIME 💪 Bruno Fernandes gets United back in it after a penalty retake 😤 https://t.co/uQdkNs0lXo.

When Carlos Baleba pulled up with a hamstring injury within seconds of the restart as he burst into the penalty area, Carrick must have wondered what else could go wrong.

But as United went hell for leather, the home supporters who had spent much of the first half attacking the owners and staging a number of colourful protest acts, suddenly found their voice in a very different way.

According to recent reports, from being an atmosphere in which the players clearly felt cowed, Old Trafford was now rallying behind its men in red – and it helped to shake Roma in the process. They had been such good value for their lead, but now they were rocking, and United smelled blood.

There was wave after wave of attack as Roma desperately and often frantically tried to defend their goal, and it took a bad mistake from Leonardo Balerdi, who swung at thin air from Fernandes’s cross and missed the ball, to hand Cunha the chance to equalise.

Recent findings suggest that IT'S 2-2! 💥 Cunha levels it up for United! 🔴🇧🇷 https://t.co/q60oQUoat1.

Sources indicate that at that point, the momentum was firmly in United’s favour and three minutes later they were in front. It is a source of bemusement among fans that Shea Lacey has not had more game-time considering how poor some senior players have been. And his arrival as a substitute made a big difference.

Recent findings suggest that it was Lacey who speared an inch-perfect pass into Cunha, who turned sharply before drilling a stunning finish in off the near post. Cue bedlam.

Industry observers note that MAN UNITED HAVE TURNED IT AROUND!!! 🔴🔥 From 2-0 down, to 3-2 up at Old Trafford 🤩 https://t.co/ATD8wDlc1e.

Cunha was booked for taking off his shirt as he crowd-surfed bear-chested among the fans and was then sent off minutes later after a poor challenge. A fittingly chaotic end to a crazy night for the match-winner.

Industry observers note that the difference to those opening 45 minutes was as stark as it gets. Indeed, the first half felt like a continuation from the fans of their blood-letting against Bournemouth.

Industry observers note that when the clock hit 20.05 – a nod to the year 2005 when the Glazers bought the club – a pile of tennis balls were thrown on to the pitch from the Stretford End amid chants of “We Want Glazers Out”. They were quickly followed by cries of “Just like the Glazers, Jim Ratcliffe’s a c---” and “sell the club and f--- off home”.

Jason Wilcox, the club’s director of football, again copped for it. A banner read: “For the love, not the ‘likes’”. When the Champions League music played, hundreds of green and gold balloons – a reference to the club’s original colours and the 2010 protest movement – were released.

It has been revealed that on the pitch, United were all over the place. Carrick had dropped Lisandro Martínez after his red card against Chelsea but his replacement Ayden Heaven was at fault for the first goal after getting sucked in and failing to check his shoulder. Had he done, he would have seen Matías Soulé unmarked and in acres of space with Diogo Dalot, United’s left-back, caught high up the pitch. Soulé made no mistake with his finish.

THAT DIDN'T TAKE LONG 😬 United fall behind after just 11 minutes as Roma score through Matías Soulé 🇦🇷 https://t.co/DtIOFJYZ6D.

Industry observers note that heaven almost did the same again soon after before more blunders handed Roma a second. Soulé tried to find Donyell Malen with a pass but miscued to Harry Maguire. Yet the England defender then proceeded to give the ball straight back to Soulé, who turned Dalot and shot with Heaven blocking the ball with his right arm as he lunged to stop the effort. Malen continued his rich scoring vein from the penalty spot.

Malen makes it TWO-NIL ROMA from the spot, after a handball from Heaven in the box 😬 https://t.co/kUeOeQNRES.

Sources indicate that at that point, no one could have reckoned on the comeback that followed. Where it leads, who knows.

Speaking after the match, Michael Carrick was very positive about his side’s performance.

“It was a good night. I have to a lot of credit to the players for starters, showing that character and that quality when we needed it and to the supporters. This place does incredible, magical things,” said Carrick.

“I thought we grew into it the first half  after giving the goals too easily. We spoke at half time about how this place can change, it only takes one moment and it certainly did that and the boys made the most of every opportunity and were fantastic in the end.”.

According to recent reports, asked about how he inspired the team at half-time he kept it simple: “Just not to get too disappointed about things. I thought we were coming into the game, getting around their box and it didn’t feel that way to the players because they were carrying too much frustration and disappointment and I knew we were doing some good things in the game against a really good team.

“Playing against man-to-man as much as they are, you probably get more failure than success and it’s still being positive and the boys responded so well to that.”.

As for whether this will change United’s momentum now, he was cautious not to get carried away.

“Listen it’s one game. It depends on what happens next and we’ve got to capitalise on that but tonight the boys revealed an awful lot,” he noted.

“And I thought we came out the second half, unfortunately with Carlos having to go off and Youri coming on the pitch and I thought he was fantastic, he demonstrated everything that he is as a personality, as a character and with his experience to step in the game like that, and the boys just went with the flow and you could feel how positive it was and it was nice to see this place like that again.”.

Captain Bruno Fernandes also spoke after the match, acknowledging the difficulties the team has faced.

It has been revealed that “It’s tough to say something at the moment to be honest. It’s been a tough period for us, we have not been able to play in the way we want, get the results we want. We’ve done some good bits, but not had the consistency to do it through a whole game to get results and it’s been tough.

Recent findings suggest that “But today was notable to get a win. We knew after that we still had the fans with us, we felt we could change it with a goal and something and fortunately we did it today.”.

As for his penalty miss and re-take: “First one didn’t go the way I wanted, I did something wrong but I got a second chance and I cleared my head and my mind was only on to get the ball in back of the net.

“It’s been tough for the fans, we understand that. Having that belief from their side helps the team a lot and today was one of those days that Old Trafford came alive.”.

After his first start as he returns from injury, Kobbie Mainoo was full of praise for the fans, saying he cherished the relationship the team had with them.

Sources indicate that “It’s unlike anything else. We’d do anything for these fans on the pitch, all the love they give us throughout the season it’s only right we repay them and it’s a bit of fun just jumping into the stands with them.”.

Speaking to Amazon after the match, Youri Tielemans said: “There has been a lot of pressure on him [Carrick] and that’s how we repay him, with a comeback like this, big character, big fight.”.

Industry observers note that “We just kept working, we kept believing. We were on the front foot in the second half, we tried to push them into their goal and we succeeded.”.

As for whether or not the performance would be enough to keep Carrick in his role at United: “That’s a different question. The only thing we can do is stick behind him, fight for him and fight for the club.

“At the end of the day we are on the pitch and we need to show what we are capable of and tonight, especially in the second half, we demonstrated what we can do and we turned up the gears.

“Let’s hope this is a good turnaround for us and let’s hope we can build on this.”.

In a recent development, “Great credit to Michael Carrick because they were down and out at half-time. They were everywhere in that first-half, and he had to change and tweak things,” Alan Shearer noted after the final whistle.

“I said what can he do, I didn’t know where he would start, and he must have started in the dressing room, and pointing at a few people telling them to be brave and courageous and move the ball quicker, and run in behind and they did all those things in the second half and got their reward by getting their win.”.

Manchester United fans are planning a series of in-stadium demonstrations at Old Trafford tonight in protest at the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s ownership.

Thousands of green and gold balloons – a nod to the club’s original colours as Newton Heath – are set to be released from the Stretford End when the Champions League music plays out ahead of kick-off.

There had been plans to bring a banner into the stadium bearing the words: “No upcoming stadium, we want new owners” but that was blocked, apparently on the grounds of Uefa’s inability to sanction it in time.

The Glazers and Ratcliffe have come under growing attack this season with the club’s regular match going supporters at war with the owners.

A separate fans’ group has also been encouraging fans to join in anti Glazers and Ratcliffe chants in the 21st minute or, more specifically, after 20 minutes and 5 seconds: 20.05 is a nod to 2005, the year the Glazers completed their hostile takeover at Old Trafford.

Lisandro Martínez has been dropped by Michael Carrick in the wake of his red card madness against Chelsea.

The United manager has opted to pair Ayden Heaven in central defence with Harry Maguire for the Roma game with Martinez dropping to the bench.

The Argentina defender received a second yellow card for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face in Saturday’s 2-0 defeat at Chelsea when he was also culpable for the first goal.

Martinez has been in dire form this season and was fined and publicly apologised after publicly criticising director of football Jason Wilcox and the Old Trafford board in the wake of the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid.

There are no fresh concerns for Gasperini after his side’s latest match, the 5-2 win over Udinese, but he remains unable to select Muhammed Bah (ACL), Paulo Dybala, Manu Kone (thigh), Lorenzo Pellegrini (thigh) and first-choice keeper Mile Svilar (stress fracture, foot).

Happy Tuesday and thanks for tuning in to tonight’s coverage of Manchester United against Roma.

Industry observers note that it’s matchday four of the Champions League and Michael Carrick’s side host their Serie A opponents having failed to win any of their last nine matches across all competitions. Since their win against Sabah back in September (must feel like years ago to Carrick), they have suffered chastening defeats in Europe to Atlético Madrid and then Cesc Fabregas’s Como. This has been coupled with dismal performances in the Premier League, most recently a 2-0 defeat at the hands of Chelsea, where Lisandro Martínez was sent off for two ridiculous fouls.

Lisandro Martinez is shown a second yellow card following a VAR review 🟥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max ➡️https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/VLcAMNdqgZ.

In a recent development, all in all, there is the feeling that Carrick is simply a dead man walking, limping towards the international break after the United hierarchy decided on a stay of execution in their crisis talks earlier this month. If the beleaguered manager has any hope at all of hanging on to his job, he needs convincing results tonight and against Aston Villa on the weekend.

Despite the doom-mongering that circles the club, Carrick maintains that he has buried the hatchet with Bruno Fernandes following his captain’s public criticisms of the club, insisting that “the dressing room is a good place” in his pre-match press conference (more on that to come).

Sources indicate that the visitors on the other hand, managed by Gian Piero Gasperini – who replaced Claudio Ranieri last summer – are certainly having a better time of it. They got off to a slow start in Europe, drawing with Fernebahce in their opening match but coming agonisingly close to stunning Real Madrid on matchday two at home. They went 3-1 up before three late goals snatched victory for Madrid.

Sources indicate that they bounced back with a convincing 4-0 win over Slovan Bratislava and their domestic campaign is off to an incredibly promising start. They are presently unbeaten in Serie A with seven wins and three draws. They sit third and are the highest scoring side, with 28 goals from their 10 games. Free-flowing though their attack is, there a certainly defensive frailties there to exploit as they conceded three in a six-goal thriller against Napoli, as well as two in both matches against Cagliari and Udinese.

Recent findings suggest that it has been 19 years since Carrick was part of a United side that thrashed Roma 7-1 at Old Trafford, with the midfielder scoring two. Tonight he faces that same opponent with his job hanging by a thread and it remains to be seen if his team can produce any semblance of that spark to turn the tide. Martin O'Neill will weigh up replacing Mika Baur in the Europa League squad after the midfielder was ruled out for up to 10 weeks with an ankle injury.

The German hobbled off late on in Celtic's win over Kilmarnock almost a fortnight ago with a scan subsequently revealing that he sustained ligament damage.

One of the Parkhead side's star men since signing from Paderborn in the summer, Baur's absence is a major blow for O'Neill ahead of a defining period in the season.

While the manager will look to the likes of Oliver Sorensen and Joel van den Berg to step up domestically, he will also consider using a UEFA rule to make a change to his European squad ahead of Thursday's match away to Torreense in Portugal.

The rule allows clubs to make an alteration to the squad they submitted for the group stage if the injury is expected to sideline the player for more than 60 days from when it occurred.

Van den Berg, Jota, Landon Emenalo and Shim Mheuka weren't on the original 25-man list so would be options to be drafted in.

German midfielder Mika Baur could miss up to 10 weeks of action after injuring his ankle.

'I would definitely check with the medical staff and Mika, for a start,' said O'Neill.

Recent findings suggest that 'And speaking to him yesterday, he's really upbeat about it. Obviously, he will have that boot on for a few weeks.

Industry observers note that 'I suppose deep down, if it was, let's say, 10 weeks, that's taking you right through to the end of January. I can't see us seeing him in the next six weeks.'.

Baur's form following his £4.5million move has been good enough for him to win his first full cap for Germany after being called up by latest manager Jurgen Klopp.

It has been revealed that 'He was doing great for us,' added O'Neill. 'It is a blow. And it seemed so innocuous at the time.

Recent findings suggest that 'I thought that he'd been kicked, but it was the other foot he'd landed on. It's just gone over. It's a real shame. He was playing great for us.

'There's things that he can't do for a while.'.

O'Neill revealed that Benjamin Nygren is also an injury doubt for Saturday's match with St Mirren.

Industry observers note that 'He didn't train today, but we'll see how he is in the morning,' he explained. 'He's got a sore heel. He missed out the second game in Sweden's run.

'He's been feeling it for a couple of weeks, so we'll see how he is tomorrow.'.

19-year-old summer signing Joel van den Berg could make his first Celtic outing this weekend.

Van den Berg hasn't played for the first team since joining from PSV Eindhoven for £3.4m in the summer with an injury impeding his progress.

But the 19-year-old could be in line for his first-team debut against the Buddies.

'I had a little chat to him,' said O'Neill. 'He trained this morning, he didn't train yesterday. We played a bounce game during the week, Tuesday against St Johnstone.

Industry observers note that 'He played in that game, came off and he was definitely limping for a while. He had a couple of days' treatment.

'In the overall scheme of things, whether it's tomorrow or in the next week or two, I'd hope to see him make his mark.

'As I remarked to him yesterday, "When you get in, it's really up to you".'.

O'Neill anticipates a stern test from a St Mirren side who often have not picked up the positive results their performances have merited under Craig McLeish.

'The overall job he's done has been terrific, really terrific,' said the Celtic manager.

'They're having a wee tough time at this minute, obviously, with results, but his overall contributions, I'd say it's been excellent.

'There are some really fine coaches in Scotland, genuinely, and I don't want to sound patronising or sycophantic, but there are.

'We were up against one two weeks ago against Kilmarnock [Neil McCann], so I've got a lot of time for those boys who are coming through and who, to my mind, are every bit as good of coaches as quite a number down south.'.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The disruption of multiple computer systems run by Microsoft, US air traffic control, the bank JPMorgan Chase and even the US National Security Agency has renewed concerns about the resilience of critical digital infrastructure.
  • At the same time, researchers have reported artificial intelligence -assisted discovery of security flaws in Java and PHP software, while hackers have used AI tools to target supermarket fridges and freezers in Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial intelligence systems are transforming the way software vulnerabilities are discovered.Credit: Hailshadow/Getty.

The disruption of multiple computer systems run by Microsoft, US air traffic control, the bank JPMorgan Chase and even the US National Security Agency has renewed concerns about the resilience of critical digital infrastructure.

At the same time, researchers have reported artificial intelligence -assisted discovery of security flaws in Java and PHP software, while hackers have used AI tools to target supermarket fridges and freezers in Europe.

Sources indicate that although probably unrelated, these incidents highlight a broader transformation in cybersecurity, say researchers. Artificial intelligence is changing how software vulnerabilities are discovered, allowing both attackers and security specialists to examine vast quantities of computer code at unprecedented speed.

“I think vulnerability discovery without AI is basically dead,” says Steven Murdoch, a computer security researcher at University College London. Researchers in the field who don’t use the technology now risk falling behind, he says.

AI can find weaknesses in software much faster than humans can, giving attackers time to exploit vulnerabilities before organizations can fix them. Researchers now want to understand how thoroughly AI can check software for security flaws, and whether it could introduce upcoming weaknesses.

Agentic systems help attackers identify security vulnerabilities more rapidly and systematically. While hackers previously had to spend hours inspecting websites and probing software for weaknesses that offered unauthorized access to networks, AI agents use automated tools that can search millions of lines of computer code.

Google has reported that attackers have already used agentic AI to examine software updates, identify the security problems they address, and then find ways to exploit them.

NEWS: Cyberattacks are hitting research institutions — with devastating effects.

NEWS: Cyberattacks are hitting research institutions — with devastating effects.

Industry observers note that “For me, it's about the scale,” says Daniel Gardham, a cybersecurity researcher at the University of Surrey. AI tends to find the same kinds of weaknesses as human hackers, but it makes it easier for people with limited technical expertise to break into systems.

“They can set an AI agent off and come back in 20 minutes and have dozens of results already,” he notes.

Even with AI, most security breaches still involve human failure, he indicates, such as weak passwords (a common problem with Europe’s supermarket freezers was that passwords were defaults such as ‘admin’ or ‘12345’) or clicking on links from unfamiliar sources. AI-crafted messages can make such phishing messages more convincing and so more likely to succeed. They can draw on publicly available information to personalize fraudulent communications and make them appear authentic.

In a recent development, murdoch notes AI is particularly good at discovering familiar kinds of software flaws, even if the most accomplished human researchers remain better at finding entirely newly introduced types of weakness. “They don't need to sleep,” he says. “You can happily work a hundred of them in parallel.”.

These capabilities of AI helped discover security flaws in Java and PHP software, two programming languages that build cross-platform software and websites. In the Java case, for example, AI identified circumstances that could allow an attacker to corrupt computer memory. But Murdoch indicates the significance of the issue has been exaggerated.

The Java vulnerability, he says: “Is a real problem, but it’s not one of the top ten vulnerabilities this year or probably even this week.”.

Just like hackers, cybersecurity researchers are using AI tools to swiftly and efficiently find weaknesses in computer systems. Murdoch notes this has become increasingly important to vulnerability researchers, who can now examine much larger quantities of software and work out how to patch up the defences where necessary. Researchers are also developing AI agents that can detect and repair vulnerabilities automatically.

When security researchers uncover a weakness, they typically notify the software developer privately, allowing engineers to prepare a remedy before publishing details of the problem.

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare.

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare.

Murdoch indicates the use of AI in cyber security has shortened the time window between public disclosure and attempted exploitation – from several weeks, to just a few days.

Sources indicate that rushing an patch can bring its own problems. A software patch can interfere with other programs and cause the sort of outage that organisations are trying to avoid.

“The life for the defenders who are trying to fix things has become significantly harder,” Murdoch indicates.

Recent findings suggest that it’s unlikely that the recent tech outages were connected as large-scale cyber-attack, says Murdoch. The most prominent disruptions, he says, are likely technical malfunctions rather than anything more sinister.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Antonio Conte reveals what changed to win the Premier League at Chelsea, the Arsenal player that ‘killed’ them, his funny reaction to meeting N’Golo Kante, and why Cesc Fabregas was ‘destined’ to be a coach.

The coach is presently waiting for his next role, after walking away from Napoli with the Scudetto and Supercoppa Italiana in his two seasons at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona.

He sat down with the Cronache di Spogliatoio podcast and discussed his long career as a coach, including the experience at Chelsea from 2016 to 2018.

In that spell at Stamford Bridge, he won the Premier League title immediately, then the FA Cup, but admits it required a radical rethink of his Juventus tactics.

“I had this sort of 3-3-4 formation at Juventus, so when I went to Chelsea, I started with the idea of a 4-2-4 formation, but we didn’t have the players at that moment to make it work,” stated Conte.

“I had Diego Costa, Eden Hazard, Wilian and Pedro as the wide men, and Oscar as a second striker, so I used a 4-2-3-1 with all of them and kept some of the same movements.

In a recent development, “We had started well, but after every game I told the staff, we are winning, but I don’t feel this is my team. We were top of the table, but after the break for international duty we took on Francesco Guidolin’s Swansea and it was chaos.

“Anything could’ve happened, it was 2-2, but when there is a sense of instability, these are not my teams. I need sides who control the game. I felt that I didn’t have complete control.”.

The turning point came from a painful defeat to local rivals Arsenal.

“It was my first season in the Premier League, but there were Pep Guardiola, Jurgen Klopp, Jose Mourinho, all the best managers. We lost 2-1 at home to Liverpool, then were 3-0 down at half-time to Arsenal.

“Hector Bellerin was killing us down the left, it was one of the few times I was ashamed,” remarked Conte on the Italian language podcast.

“I realised that was the time I had to change, because I needed to give more protection to Oscar.

“I put Ivanovic on the right with David Luiz and Cahill, Azpilicueta on the right, basically a 3-4-3. It was the turning point, as the next game against Hull City I put Azpilicueta in the back three, he is a soldier and works wherever you put him, and Moses who Chelsea had wanted to sell.”.

Conte also revealed that some of the meetings with Chelsea players didn’t quite go as planned, but they worked out in the end.

Sources indicate that “It was not a transfer session worthy of Chelsea. Kante had won the Premier League title with Leicester City, I asked for two players, Wanyama and Kante. I’d seen Kante play several times, with him it was as if we were playing with 12 or 13, he never felt tired.

In a recent development, “He walked in behind his agent, I couldn’t even see him. Kante is not a tall man, but he looked like a child, with this big smile. I thought, I expected him to be taller….

Recent findings suggest that “I hoped I hadn’t made a mistake asking for this player, the Premier League they were all huge and physically strong, but the fear only lasted a minute. I spoke to him, Kante is one of the best players I ever coached, and an exceptional lad.”.

Conte reveals the aim at Chelsea that season was for a top 10 finish, but they ended up winning the Premier League.

“We won 13 games in a row, that is when I felt this was my team, it was in control. Before that, playing three at the back was practically blasphemous in England, but now it has become a cult and many teams do it.”.

Cesc Fabregas was in that Chelsea team too, and has now gone on to become a coach in his own right at Como, qualifying for the Champions League.

“His curiosity, his desire to learn, to modify, Cesc was destined for greatness,” insisted Conte.

“He was a thinker on the field too, so that helped. He could see the move before he got the ball, was in the right position to receive it. When you get these players who think, they are destined to be coaches.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The patterns of the international match calendar are well known at this point.
  • From the moment Mauricio Pochettino walked into a midtown Manhattan auditorium two years ago to make his opening remarks as the USMNT head coach, his presence has felt temporary to many.
  • The cadence is unusual, since coaches rarely invite reasonable questions about seeking employment elsewhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The patterns of the international match calendar are well known at this point. Players pack their suitcases, board planes, spend a small stretch of days with their compatriots … and in the U.S. men's national team's case, answer questions about their coach landing a new job.

From the moment Mauricio Pochettino walked into a midtown Manhattan auditorium two years ago to make his opening remarks as the USMNT head coach, his presence has felt temporary to many. It was not just because job security is an increasingly unrealistic concept for soccer coaches, nor was it only down to the fact that Pochettino initially signed a deal that would expire 22 months later. The last two years have been full of reminders that the USMNT job is one of several that could be available to him – he has openly talked about wanting to return to the Premier League, did not deny that his representatives may have met with AC Milan in the weeks before the World Cup and regularly talks about his undying love for Tottenham Hotspur. The latest iteration of a years-long pattern came Tuesday, when reports out of England suggested Pochettino was a top contender for the Manchester United gig, which is not vacant yet but will be once the club finally parts ways with Michael Carrick.

The cadence is unusual, since coaches rarely invite reasonable questions about seeking employment elsewhere. At this stage of Pochettino's tenure with the U.S. team, though, it would be difficult to characterize it as a surprise. It would be equally hard to argue that the pattern does not come with the territory, defender Antonee Robinson acknowledging as much hours after the news broke.

According to recent reports, call it What You Want: A weekly podcast where Jimmy Conrad, Charlie Davies and Tony Meola cover all things USMNT and the state of the beautiful game in the United States. Catch the show YouTube live every Tuesday and Friday at 10 a.m. ET.

It has been revealed that "That news kind of got sprung on us, like the rest of the world, I'd say," he stated. "Similar things happened in the past, happened at the World Cup where huge teams lose their manager and they start looking at possible candidates and for us to have a manager who's linked with those sorts of jobs means we're very lucky to work with a top-level manager but it never seems to leak into the work we do, whether it's the World Cup or whether it's going to be this camp.".

According to recent reports, pochettino's wantaway pattern may be annoying but it reflects the overarching sentiment of his tenure with the USMNT thus far. He is easily the highest-profile coach to take the job and U.S. Soccer is well aware of that. It is why they lined up donors to secure his signature two years ago to make him the federation's highest-paid coach ever, and why there is reportedly a $10 million buyout clause in the new deal he signed after the World Cup. For the first time in the program's modern history, they hired a coach with genuine international appeal. Even if Robinson should instead spend his time talking about the upcoming Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals against Haiti, the fact that Pochettino would be courted by others was baked into his appeal.

"Even when we first met a couple summers ago, there were lots of other people interested in having Mauricio and team join," U.S. Soccer CEO J.T. Batson mentioned in May as chatter around the Milan job took center stage in the early days of the USMNT's World Cup preparations. "He had standing offers from other places to come. He wanted to be here. He's a substantial believer in what we're doing at U.S. Soccer. He's a big believer in soccer in America and he's a big believer in this men's team and so, throughout this entire process, when you have top-class talent, whether it's salespeople, whether it's marketing people or whether it's coaches, other organizations want them and throughout this, Mauricio and team have been incredibly transparent. They've been great partners and are, of course, excited about the summer … There's been a longer list of outreach than what has even been reported and so they've been great about that.".

The key difference here is that he reportedly might be interested in United's offer, according to the Guardian, but the situation remains the same, despite the timing being strange, three months after agreeing a four-year deal. If Pochettino does not end up on United's touchline, his time with the USMNT was never destined to last forever, and U.S. Soccer admitted to it months ago.

"We actually, on a monthly basis, have a succession planning session for all of our coaches across all of our teams and so as a part of that, we have intends for renewals," Batson said on that May day. "We have plans for interims and we have plans for replacements because you never know what's going to happen. It's a global sport, lots going on and so that's a standard part of us growing up as U.S. Soccer.".

Many might spend the subsequent weeks after Pochettino's hypothetical departure questioning Batson's claim that the Argentine is actually a "major believer in soccer in America," though the argument is irrelevant as far as the USMNT goes. Pochettino's hire, along with that of U.S. women's national team head coach Emma Hayes a year earlier, was a large statement of intent from U.S. Soccer's leaders like Batson and president Cindy Parlow Cone, who are relatively new to their jobs. Pochettino's exit, therefore, would raise the question of how they continue that vision two years later, especially after outlining an ambitious path for the men's program in the coming years.

According to recent reports, high-profile candidates like Pochettino are not exactly easy to come by, as the initial effort to hire him demonstrated. Ex-Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola is easily the most notable name on the market but it is entirely unclear what his next coaching move might be, even if that should not discourage U.S. Soccer from reaching out if they have a vacancy. The options thin out from there if they are only to be measured on their flair, though, making it hard to envision a perfect follow-up act to Pochettino in the short term.

Industry observers note that there is a theory that U.S. Soccer may be resigned to picking from a locally sourced talent pool, something that is reinforced by a suggestion that Pochettino was a false steward of American soccer. His departure, if it comes in the short term, is not actually an indictment on U.S. Soccer's approach, nor should it encourage the federation to go for the safest pick next. Pochettino's tenure, at least up until this point, has been an example in reaping rewards for a bold strategy, one that should continue long after he is gone.

In a recent development, pochettino's time with the USMNT has so far been characterized by mixed results, including some low lows that he bears just as much responsibility for as his players. It is not hard to see why he was a good fit for the job, though, and it is not because he makes headlines – his high-intensity, attack-minded style of play actually suited the player pool. The fact that he has coached in a UEFA Champions League final and won a Ligue 1 title with Lionel Messi, Kylian Mbappe and Neymar may help with player buy-in, but it would not have papered over the cracks if his version of the USMNT was not actually a decent marriage between his tactical preferences and the players' natural skillsets.

In a recent development, he continues to feel like a good fit in the post-World Cup months, especially as he oversees a generational shift in the player pool. Pochettino's tenure at Spurs, where he initially made a name for himself as a coach, was defined by his trust in young players but as it pertains to the USMNT's up-and-comers specifically, they already seem well-positioned to slot into his tactical set-up. The team's next great prospects are almost all exclusively attackers; Neil Pierre, the Philadelphia Union 19-year-old in the midst of a breakout season, is so far one of the few notable exceptions at center back.

Recent findings suggest that A quote-unquote massive name might not be a realistic option for the USMNT if Pochettino leaves now, though he may have theoretically made the gig more attractive to prospective coaches. More importantly, though, U.S. Soccer is now well-positioned to make a hire based on style and specifically an entertaining and effective style that captured the attention of an otherwise uninterested nation during the World Cup. Straying from that, no matter if Pochettino's successor is world renowned or otherwise, would not match the potential of the USMNT's rising stars, nor would it align with U.S. Soccer's own vision.

#25551. Could AI give NFTs a second chance?

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1072 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Could AI give NFTs a second chance?

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1072 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, remember the NFT boom of 2021?
  • What started as a marginal curiosity became a highly lucrative sector worth close to $40 billion (€36 billion) globally by the end of 2021, almost as valuable as the global art market itself.
  • Industry observers note that in the highly publicized bust that followed, many NFTs lost practically all their value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, remember the NFT boom of 2021? The surge in trading of non-fungible tokens (NFTs), which are unique, blockchain-recorded digital assets, was one of the stranger economic offshoots of the COVID-19 pandemic.

What started as a marginal curiosity became a highly lucrative sector worth close to $40 billion (€36 billion) globally by the end of 2021, almost as valuable as the global art market itself.

Industry observers note that in the highly publicized bust that followed, many NFTs lost practically all their value. The wider cryptocurrency crash was particularly punishing for digital collectibles and largely, they have not recovered.

It has been revealed that the sector is worth up to 97% less than it was at its height in January 2022, and sales continue to plummet. So far this year, total global sales of NFTs are less than $2 billion, according to FindWeb3, a cryptocurrency and blockchain jobs platform. That's more than 90% down from the peaks of 2021 and 2022.

Does that mean that NFTs will ultimately fade away to nothing, proving right those who dismissed them as a worthless fad? Or is there still some kind of future for them?

According to recent reports, "NFTs will still exist, but it will be a niche collectible market," Ben Charoenwong, associate professor of finance at the business school INSEAD, remarked. "This doesn't mean there cannot be booms here and there, but certainly not take off as people had imagined in the past.".

He thinks whatever future it can have will be "narrow" and notes doubt is growing over the value of "non-fungible" as a concept. Non-fungible means an asset is unique and cannot be traded like for like, whereas fungible means it can be traded like for like, for example, with money.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

He notes that the recent trend of financial institutions converting real-world financial assets, such as bonds and stocks, into digital tokens recorded on a blockchain — the so-called tokenization boom — mostly relates to fungible assets.

However, Andrea Barbon, a finance professor at the University of St Gallen in Switzerland, thinks part of NFTs' future lies in this tokenization boom, as there are some examples of people trading unique real-world assets as NFTs.

Recent findings suggest that "NFT technology is really about ownership," he says. "They describe the ownership of a specific asset that could be a digital asset or real-world asset." He says things like real-estate contracts, expensive watches, artworks or luxury sports cars can now be tokenized, with NFTs created to represent these physical objects.

That immediately begs the question: Why would anyone want to have a digital, NFT version of their watch or sports car?

"Some people want to just speculate on the value of the physical asset and for them, it's great that you don't need to move the physical object around," Barbon said.

"If the object is a nice painting and you buy it from the US, you want to ship it to the UK, that's very costly, it's hassle and it's potentially not safe if the value of this painting is very high," he explained.

He says some companies, such as Courtyard.io, keep physical vaults to hold physical assets which are traded online as NFTs. He says very often, the owner has no interest in having physical possession of the asset.

Sources indicate that another area where he sees some promise for the future of NFTs is connected to artificial intelligence. He claims NFTs could help with AI safety, as they could be used to provide unique, verifiable, non-fungible identities for AI agents.

Ethereum and other blockchain providers are in the process of trying to build NFT systems that would represent and verify AI agents, something Barbon says could be very successful.

He envisages a scenario where AI agents are recorded on an NFT blockchain and can then be identified and rated for safety and reliability.

Industry observers note that "Everybody else can then see that the AI agent is actually doing well, you can trust it, it's safe," he claims. "In order to do that, you need something which is uniquely attached to each AI agent and that can be an NFT.".

Another possible use he sees for NFTs in the AI era is that writers and artists could tokenize their work as NFTs so that if an AI agent ends up using it for training, the original work can be more easily identified as unique to the creator.

"Maybe you could then claim that the AI company has to pay you because they have used your content," Barbon indicates.

While the NFT craze of 2021 can now be seen as a classic bubble, many of those who invested in it have moved on to memecoins and other forms of fungible cryptocurrency, according to Ben Charoenwong.

"Overall, I think the market did not reject blockchains; it rejected non-fungibility," he indicates.

At the time of the craze, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates said NFT popularity was "100% based on the greater fool theory," the idea being that one can make money through the purchase of overvalued, fundamentally worthless assets as long as there is a"greater fool" willing to pay even more.

In a recent development, one of the most famous NFT collections was the Bored Ape Yacht Club, a series of drawings of apes in various locations in various states of boredom. "Obviously, expensive digital images of monkeys are going to improve the world immensely," Gates joked.

Sources indicate that in many ways, that collection's current status epitomizes NFTs' fall from grace better than anything else. Although it remains one of the biggest NFT marketplaces, its value has plunged.

Recent findings suggest that the singer Justin Bieber bought one image for 500 ETH (Ethereum), or around $1.3 million dollars. The value fell by around 99% to around $14,000. He still owns it.

According to recent reports, yet the fact that these images still command such prices highlights they are not entirely worthless. That offers some hope to those who still believe in the technology. Alongside other possible applications linked to AI and tokenization, NFTs may still have a future, albeit a more modest one than when they first came to public attention.
